questions.text: Explain recursion and why the base case terminates the call stack.
questions.correct_answer: A base case is a terminating condition in a recursive function that returns a value directly without making further recursive calls, preventing stack overflow.

questions.text: Explain the difference between stack and heap memory allocation in C.
questions.correct_answer: Stack memory is automatically managed for local variables and function calls, while heap memory is manually allocated via malloc() and persists until freed.

questions.text: Explain how the base case works in recursion and write a recursive function Node* reverse(Node* head) in C to reverse a singly linked list.
Explain recursion and the importance of a base case.
questions.correct_answer: A recursive function calls itself on smaller inputs until reaching a base case condition which stops further recursive calls and returns the base result.

submissions.feedback: Your answer does not clearly explain how stack frames pop off the call stack when the terminating condition is met.
Your implementation invokes reverse(head->next) without validating if head == NULL || head->next == NULL. This causes a segmentation fault on empty or 1-node lists.

submissions.answer_text: Recursion is when a function calls itself. If head == NULL return head, then reverse rest.
submissions.misconception_group: Base case omission or improper termination
submissions.feedback: Your solution terminates when head is null, but fails to check single-node list termination (head->next == null).

submissions.answer_text: Node* reverse(Node* head) { if (head == NULL || head->next == NULL) return head; Node* rest = reverse(head->next); head->next->next = head; head->next = NULL; return rest; }
submissions.feedback: Excellent answer! You correctly handled base case boundaries and pointer unwinding.
